Read ratios carefully

A rising ratio means the numerator gained relative to the denominator; a falling ratio means it weakened. It does not reveal the cause and does not guarantee the next price move.

Different markets close at different times. GoldAlert only combines observations with a common calendar date and shows the latest shared date on each tool.

Why ratios matter more than absolute prices

A single price number tells you what something costs today, but it does not tell you whether that asset is becoming more or less valuable relative to another. That is where ratios earn their place in macro analysis. When gold rises from $2,000 to $3,000 per ounce, it looks like a big move in isolation. But if silver has risen proportionally, the gold/silver ratio has not changed — meaning the relationship between the two metals is the same as before. Only by dividing one by the other can you see which is gaining or losing ground in relative terms.

This relative-strength framing is particularly useful for cross-asset comparisons that span different unit scales. Bitcoin is priced in tens of thousands of dollars, gold in thousands, silver in tens, copper in a few dollars per pound. Comparing these directly is meaningless — the Bitcoin/Gold ratio strips away the unit problem and shows you purely how the two assets are moving relative to each other.

The ratios on this panel and what each shows

The Gold/Silver ratio is one of the oldest tracked financial relationships, showing how many ounces of silver equal one ounce of gold. A high ratio (silver cheap relative to gold) often accompanies risk-off environments. A low ratio often accompanies commodity bull markets. The Gold/Copper ratio compares a defensive monetary metal with an industrial-demand bellwether, making it a proxy for risk sentiment and economic cycle positioning. The Gold/Platinum ratio shows the historical inversion between these two precious metals — platinum once traded above gold, but gold's monetary premium has made the ratio sit well above 1.0 since 2011. The Gold/Oil ratio links financial and energy markets, reflecting how much monetary and safe-haven value gold carries relative to the cost of energy. The Bitcoin/Gold ratio is the newest addition: it captures the rivalry and complementarity between the original store of value and the digital challenger.

How GoldAlert aligns dates for ratio calculations

Gold, silver, copper, oil and Bitcoin all trade on different venues with different trading hours, holiday schedules and closing conventions. A naively calculated ratio that divides today's gold close by yesterday's copper close (because copper had a holiday) would introduce a timing error into the ratio. GoldAlert avoids this by using only aligned calendar dates — dates where both components have a confirmed closing price — and publishing the latest shared date on each ratio page so the methodology is fully transparent.

Each ratio page also includes an indicator showing whether the ratio has moved higher or lower over the most recent session where a reading is available. This directional signal shows momentum, not a recommendation.
